question: does raising the adversarial sample size make the McNemar test significant?
short_answer: yes, but only after fixing two scoring artifacts that were fabricating discordant pairs; and the effect is concentrated in one task family

step1_power_analysis.conclusion: on these task families the generator error rate is 0, so more samples of the same kind cannot create discordant pairs; a different task family or a weaker generator model is required

step3_scoring_fix.artifact: records with status=incomplete (output budget consumed by reasoning) had no answer text; a literal matcher scores them as wrong
step3_scoring_fix.why_it_matters: the handicap was asymmetric: B1 must reason from scratch while B2 can lean on the evidence, so B1 ran out of budget far more often
step3_scoring_fix.fix: scorable() requires call_succeeded AND answer_was_produced; no-answer rows are counted in excluded, never scored as wrong

step4_harness_repair.note: only rows with no answer were dropped and re-run; rows that already produced an answer were untouched, so this removes a handicap rather than selecting samples

interpretation: the whole effect sits in identity-constant, where the generator is 100% correct but B1 reasons its way to a wrong answer on implementation-dependent identity; B2, shown the real stdout, keeps it right. This is the harmful-self-review regime from table 10-1 and Huang et al. ICLR 2024, not the execution-feedback-fixes-errors regime. The other three families show no difference at all because the generator is already perfect on them.
honest_limits: the identity-constant family is small (18 pairs) and was curated after screening
the overall p=0.0117 rests on 10 discordant pairs, 7 of which come from that family
B2 can transcribe the stdout, so 100% accuracy there is partly cheap
the repair changed the output budget for 17 B1 rows; results are conditional on it
